science.model_version: Multi-Force Work-Energy Ledger Model v1 (W_net = sum(W_i) = Delta K)

self_teaching_test.learner_can_explain: A learner must explain how individual collinear and inclined forces contribute signed work components to change kinetic energy, and recognize why perpendicular forces do zero work.
self_teaching_test.novice_dependency_check: A novice must understand Newton's second law F = ma and vector projection W = F*d*cos(theta) before setting up a multi-force ledger.
self_teaching_test.unassisted_question: A 5 kg sled slides 4 m down a 30° slope with 10 N friction while pulled downward by 15 N along the slope. What is its net work?
self_teaching_test.expected_reasoning: Work components along displacement: W_pull = +15 * 4 = +60 J, friction work W_fric = -10 * 4 = -40 J, and gravity work W_grav = m * g * (d * sin 30°) = 5 * 10 * (4 * 0.5) = +100 J. Summing all components: W_net = 60 - 40 + 100 = +120 Joules.
self_teaching_test.counterfactual_reasoning: A novice might erroneously use total slope distance 4 m in the gravity calculation without multiplying by sin 30°, predicting W_grav = 5 * 10 * 4 = 200 J and incorrectly inflating the net work to 220 J.

core1b.anchor_problem: A 2 kg box is already moving right at 1 m/s. A child pulls it horizontally to the right with a constant 10 N force, while friction is 4 N to the left. It travels 3 m. What is the net work done on the box, and what is its final speed?
core1b.new_problem: A 3 kg model scooter starts from rest at the bottom of a 2 m slope rising 0.5 m. A motor provides a constant 15 N uphill force, while friction is a constant 3 N downhill. The ramp normal force is perpendicular to movement. Take g = 10 m s^-2. Determine whether the scooter reaches the top and calculate its speed at the top.
core1b.anchor_crux: W_pull = +10 * 3 = +30 J. W_fric = -4 * 3 = -12 J. Normal force and gravity act perpendicular to dis
core1b.new_crux: Motor work: W_mot = +15 * 2 = +30 J. Friction work: W_fric = -3 * 2 = -6 J. Gravity work: W_grav = -
core1b.numeric_swap_rejected: The anchor problem solves a simple horizontal crate pull with friction, while the Core1B transfer introduces an inclined ramp requiring simultaneous resolution of uphill motor force, downhill friction, and vertical gravity elevation change.

stages.predict: Predict whether the scooter can reach the top of the ramp when motor force, friction, and gravity all act concurrently.
stages.attempt: Evaluate all four force work components and determine whether net work is positive and what final speed is reached.
stages.reconstruct: Demonstrate that motor work (+30 J), friction (-6 J), and gravity (-15 J) sum to +9 J, yielding v = sqrt(2*9/3) = sqrt(6) ≈ 2.45 m/s.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether the error was calculating gravity along the hypotenuse or assuming normal force does work.
stages.repair: Recall that normal force is perpendicular to motion (W_N = 0) and gravity depends strictly on vertical elevation change (W_g = -m*g*Delta h).
stages.boundary_test: Find the minimum motor force for the scooter to just reach the top with zero speed, verifying F_mot = 10.5 N.

hints.H1: First calculate the separate work done by motor, friction, and gravity along the 2 m path.
hints.H2: Recall that gravity work depends only on vertical elevation change: W_grav = -m * g * Delta h.
hints.H3: Sum all three work contributions to find W_net = Delta K, then solve for v_f.

multiple_subtopic_main.integrated_reasoning: Combines multi-force work ledger (W01) with spring elasticity (W02) and constant power motor dynamics (W03) across a composite test track.
